title: Finish dinner three hours before bed
body: When you lie down soon after a meal, stomach acid can flow back up into the food pipe. This is one of the commonest reasons for night-time heartburn and a sour taste in the morning.
try: If you sleep at 11 pm, aim to finish dinner by 8 pm. Keep late-night snacks light.

title: Sugary drinks feed fatty liver
body: Soft drinks, packaged juices and sweetened tea or coffee deliver a large dose of sugar that the liver turns into fat. Regular sugary drinks are closely linked with fatty liver, even in people who are not overweight.
try: Swap one sugary drink a day for plain water, unsweetened chaas or nimbu pani without sugar.

title: Most of us eat too little fibre
body: Adults need about 25 to 30 grams of fibre a day for regular, comfortable bowels. Diets built on white rice, maida and packaged foods usually fall well short.
try: Add one high-fibre food today: a bowl of sprouts, whole dal, a fruit with its peel, or atta with the chokar left in. Increase slowly and drink more water.

title: Tea or coffee on an empty stomach
body: For people prone to acidity, strong tea or coffee as the very first thing in the morning can trigger burning and nausea.
try: Eat something small first, such as a fruit, a few soaked almonds or a roti, then have your tea.

title: ORS comes first in loose motions
body: The main danger of diarrhoea is losing water and salts, not the infection itself. ORS replaces both better than plain water, juice or soft drinks.
try: Keep a few ORS packets at home. If you have none, mix 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of salt in 1 litre of clean water. See a doctor if there is blood, high fever or very little urine.

title: Detox and herbal products can harm the liver
body: Some unregulated herbal powders, weight-loss products, body-building supplements and 'liver tonics' can cause serious liver injury. Natural does not always mean safe.
try: Tell your doctor about every supplement, powder or home remedy you take, including the ones you think are harmless.

title: Why healthy foods can cause gas
body: Rajma, chana, onion, garlic, cabbage and cauliflower contain carbohydrates that gut bacteria ferment. In people with a sensitive gut, this causes bloating and gas.
try: Soak legumes overnight, discard the water and pressure-cook well. Eat smaller portions rather than cutting these foods out completely.

title: Jaundice from water: hepatitis A and E
body: Hepatitis A and E spread through contaminated water and food, and they are a common cause of jaundice in India, especially after the monsoon.
try: Drink boiled or properly filtered water. Avoid cut fruit and pani puri water from roadside stalls. Ask your doctor about the hepatitis A vaccine for children.

title: Spicy food does not cause ulcers
body: Most stomach ulcers are caused by the H. pylori infection or by painkillers. Spicy food can worsen burning in someone who already has gastritis, but it does not create an ulcer.
try: If you have upper stomach pain that keeps coming back, ask about an H. pylori test instead of only avoiding chillies.

title: Small weight loss, big liver benefit
body: Losing 7 to 10 percent of your body weight can reduce liver fat and even reverse early scarring. For a person weighing 80 kg, that is 6 to 8 kg.
try: Aim for a steady loss of half to one kilo a week through smaller portions and daily walking. Crash diets are not needed.

title: How to take isabgol correctly
body: Isabgol (psyllium husk) is a safe fibre supplement for constipation, but it needs enough water to work. Taken with too little water, it can make constipation worse.
try: Start with one teaspoon stirred into a full glass of water, drink it straight away, then drink another glass of water.

title: Milk, curd and bloating
body: Many Indian adults digest milk sugar (lactose) less well as they age, which causes gas and loose stools after milk. Curd, buttermilk and paneer contain much less lactose and are usually better tolerated.
try: If milk bloats you, try a smaller cup taken with a meal, or switch to curd or chaas.

title: There is no liver-friendly alcohol
body: Every type of alcohol, including wine and beer, adds load to the liver. For people with fatty liver, hepatitis B or C, or cirrhosis, even small regular amounts speed up damage.
try: If you have any liver condition, the safest amount of alcohol is none.

title: Painkillers and your stomach
body: Common painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin can cause stomach ulcers and bleeding, especially in older people and when taken often.
try: Take them only when needed, after food, for the shortest time. Ask your doctor for a gentler option if you need pain relief regularly.

title: Use your morning reflex
body: Eating breakfast naturally triggers the bowel to move. Ignoring that urge repeatedly is a common cause of constipation.
try: Sit on the toilet for 5 to 10 minutes after breakfast, without your phone. Resting your feet on a small stool to raise your knees makes passing stool easier.

title: Swap maida for whole grains
body: White bread, biscuits, noodles and other maida products have had most of their fibre removed. They digest fast and do little for your bowels or blood sugar.
try: Choose whole-wheat roti, brown or hand-pounded rice, oats, millets like bajra and ragi, and keep the chokar in your atta.

title: Raise the head of your bed
body: For night-time reflux, raising the head end of the bed by 6 to 8 inches helps gravity keep acid down. Extra pillows only bend the neck and do not work as well.
try: Place bricks or wooden blocks under the legs at the head end of your bed.

title: Coffee and the liver
body: Regular coffee drinkers have a lower risk of liver scarring in many large studies. The benefit is linked to plain coffee, not sugary coffee drinks.
try: If you enjoy coffee, one or two cups a day with little or no sugar is fine for most people with fatty liver.

title: Black stools: what is harmless and what is not
body: Iron tablets and some foods can make stools dark, which is harmless. Stools that are black, sticky and tar-like, especially with weakness or dizziness, can mean bleeding in the stomach.
try: Tar-like black stools with weakness need care the same day. If you are on iron tablets and feel well, mention it at your next visit.

title: Crash diets can cause gallstones
body: Losing weight very fast, or skipping meals for long periods, changes bile and raises the chance of gallstones forming.
try: Lose weight steadily and eat regular, moderate meals rather than long fasts followed by heavy ones.

title: Breaking a fast gently
body: After a long fast, a large fried or very sweet meal can trigger acidity, bloating, and in people with gallstones, a painful attack.
try: Break a fast with water, fruit or a light dish first, and have the main meal a little later.

title: Diabetes and fatty liver go together
body: More than half of people with type 2 diabetes have fatty liver, and they are more likely to develop liver scarring.
try: If you have diabetes, ask your doctor whether your liver has been checked with a blood test and a liver stiffness test.

title: Blood in the stool is not always piles
body: Piles are common, but bleeding can also come from a fissure, polyps, inflammation or, less often, colon cancer, which is increasingly seen in younger adults.
try: Get any rectal bleeding checked once, at any age, especially if it comes with a change in bowel habit or tiredness.

title: Water and constipation
body: Fibre absorbs water to keep stools soft. Without enough fluid, more fibre can actually make stools harder.
try: Drink enough through the day to keep your urine pale yellow, and a little more in hot weather or when you increase fibre.

title: Eating after pancreatitis
body: After an attack of pancreatitis, small low-fat meals are easier on the pancreas while it recovers. Alcohol and smoking both raise the chance of another attack.
try: Choose steamed, boiled or lightly cooked food over fried food, and stop alcohol and smoking completely.

title: Hepatitis B vaccine is for adults too
body: Hepatitis B can cause lifelong liver disease, and adults who were not vaccinated as children are still at risk. The vaccine is safe and given as three doses.
try: Check whether you have had the hepatitis B vaccine. If not, or if you are unsure, ask your doctor about a blood test and vaccination.

title: Festive sweets and food safety
body: Milk-based sweets spoil quickly, and stomach infections rise during the festive season.
try: Buy sweets fresh from a reliable shop, keep them refrigerated, and throw away anything that smells or tastes sour.

title: Festive meals without the acidity
body: Fried snacks, sweets and late dinners together are a common recipe for heartburn during festivals.
try: Have the heavier meal earlier in the day, eat slowly, and take a short walk afterwards instead of lying down.

title: A short walk after meals
body: A gentle 10 to 15 minute walk after eating helps the stomach empty and lowers the rise in blood sugar after the meal.
try: Walk after lunch or dinner today. Keep it gentle; strenuous exercise right after eating can cause cramps.

title: Smoking harms the whole gut
body: Smoking worsens reflux, slows ulcer healing, makes Crohn's disease more severe, and raises the risk of cancers of the food pipe, stomach, pancreas and colon.
try: If you smoke, quitting is one of the best things you can do for your digestion. Ask your doctor about help to stop.

title: Cold milk does not cure acidity
body: Cold milk can soothe the burning for a few minutes. Its fat and protein then make the stomach release more acid, so the burning often comes back.
try: When heartburn starts, sip plain water, sit upright and avoid lying down. If you need relief several times a week, see your doctor.

title: Share the Diwali sweet boxes
body: Mithai is rich in sugar and ghee, and dry fruits are healthy but very high in calories. Finishing several boxes over a few days puts a heavy load of sugar and fat on the liver.
try: Keep to one or two pieces of mithai a day and a small handful of dry fruits. Share or pass on the rest.

title: Avoid reusing frying oil
body: Oil heated again and again for frying breaks down and forms harmful compounds. These are linked with heart disease, liver disease and some cancers.
try: Use leftover frying oil only for regular cooking within a day or two, and do not fry in it again. Throw away oil that has turned dark, thick or smoky.

title: Check cold medicines for hidden paracetamol
body: Colds become common as winter sets in, and many cold, flu and headache medicines already contain paracetamol. Taking one of these along with a separate paracetamol tablet can push the total above the safe limit and seriously harm the liver.
try: Read the label of every cold or pain medicine at home, and take only one product containing paracetamol at a time. Ask a doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure.

title: Fill half your plate with vegetables
body: Vegetables add fibre, water and nutrients with few calories, which helps the bowels, weight and fatty liver. Most Indian meals are heavy on rice or roti and light on sabzi.
try: At lunch today, fill half your plate with sabzi or salad, a quarter with dal, paneer, egg or chicken, and a quarter with roti or rice.

title: A bigger waist pushes acid up
body: Extra fat around the belly presses on the stomach and pushes acid up into the food pipe. Tight belts and waistbands after a meal add to the same pressure.
try: Loosen tight belts after meals and measure your waist today. For Indian adults, a waist above 90 cm in men or 80 cm in women is worth bringing down.

title: Go easy on pickles and papad
body: Diets high in salt and salt-preserved foods are linked with a higher risk of stomach cancer, especially in people with the H. pylori infection. Pickles, papad, namkeen and many packaged snacks carry far more salt than we realise.
try: Keep pickle to a small spoon at one meal a day, and taste your food before adding extra salt.

title: Make the most of winter greens
body: Sarson, methi, palak and bathua are in season now and are rich in fibre, iron and folate. Soil and germs cling to leafy vegetables, so they need careful washing.
try: Add one katori of saag or methi to a meal today. Wash the leaves under running water two or three times before chopping.

title: Sleep on your left side
body: The stomach lies to the left of the food pipe. Lying on your left side keeps the stomach's opening above the acid, so less of it flows back up at night. Lying on the right side tends to make night-time reflux worse.
try: If heartburn wakes you at night, start the night lying on your left side. A pillow behind your back helps you stay that way.

title: Eat the fruit, skip the juice
body: Juicing removes most of the fibre and packs the sugar of several fruits into one glass. Whole fruit fills you up, slows the rise in blood sugar and helps your bowels.
try: Have an orange, a guava or an apple whole today in place of a glass of juice.

title: Get tested once for hepatitis C
body: Hepatitis C can silently damage the liver for years before any symptoms appear. It spreads through blood, for example reused needles, unsafe injections, old blood transfusions and shared razors. Tablet treatment now clears the virus in most people.
try: Ask your doctor for a one-time hepatitis C blood test, especially if you have ever had a blood transfusion, dialysis or injections with reused needles.

title: Do not leave cooked rice out overnight
body: Some germs in rice survive cooking and multiply when cooked rice sits at room temperature for hours. They make toxins that reheating does not destroy, and these can cause sudden vomiting and loose motions.
try: Cool leftover rice and put it in the fridge within an hour or two of cooking. Eat it within a day and reheat it until it is steaming hot.

title: Add protein to your breakfast
body: Many Indian breakfasts, such as poha, paratha, or bread and biscuits with tea, are mostly carbohydrate. Protein keeps you full for longer, cuts down snacking and helps protect muscle when you are losing weight for fatty liver.
try: Add one protein food to breakfast today: curd, a besan chilla, sprouts, paneer or an egg.

title: Night-time itching may be worms
body: Threadworms are common in children. They lay eggs around the anus at night, which causes itching and disturbed sleep. The eggs stick to fingers and nails, so the whole family can catch them.
try: Keep nails short, wash hands with soap after the toilet and before meals, and wash bedsheets in hot water. If a child has itching at night, see a doctor, as everyone in the house may need treatment.

title: Keep packaged snacks occasional
body: Chips, namkeen, biscuits and instant noodles are high in salt, refined flour and fat, and low in fibre. Eating them daily is linked with weight gain, fatty liver and constipation.
try: Replace today's packaged snack with roasted chana, a fruit or a bowl of sprouts chaat.

title: Exercise lowers liver fat on its own
body: Regular physical activity reduces fat in the liver even when the weighing scale hardly moves. Both brisk walking and muscle-strengthening exercise help, and the benefit lasts as long as you keep it up.
try: Plan 30 minutes of brisk walking on five days this week, and add simple squats or stair climbing on two of them.

title: A handful of nuts, not a bowl
body: Almonds, walnuts, peanuts and seeds give healthy fats, protein and fibre, and a small daily portion is good for the heart and liver. They are also rich in calories, so large amounts in winter add weight quickly.
try: Keep today's nuts to one small handful, about what fits in your closed palm, and choose them unsalted and unfried.

title: Gurpurab langar and a comfortable stomach
body: Gurpurab falls on 24 November this year. Langar of dal, roti and sabzi is a simple, balanced meal, but long hours of seva without water, and extra fried snacks and sweets through the day, often bring heaviness and acidity.
try: Drink water regularly during seva, eat langar at your usual meal time, and keep the extra fried snacks at home to a small plate.

title: Do not hold back the urge
body: The urge to pass stool is a signal that comes and goes. If you keep ignoring it because of work, travel or an unfamiliar toilet, the stool stays longer in the bowel and becomes harder, and the urge itself gets weaker over time.
try: Go when you feel the urge today, even at work. If office toilets put you off, plan a calm few minutes at home after breakfast.

title: Learn your own heartburn triggers
body: Common triggers include fried food, chocolate, peppermint, citrus fruits, tomato gravies, onion and alcohol, but each person reacts to only a few of them. Avoiding everything on the list makes meals dull without adding much benefit.
try: For one week, note what you ate before each episode of heartburn, then cut back only on the two or three foods that show up most.

title: A swallowed button battery is an emergency
body: Small round batteries from remotes, toys, watches and weighing scales can burn through a child's food pipe within two hours. The child may look completely well at first, so waiting to see is dangerous.
try: Check that every remote and toy at home has a screwed-shut battery cover, and keep spare batteries out of reach. See a doctor at once, in an emergency department, if you think a child has swallowed a battery or a magnet.

title: Eat safely at wedding buffets
body: Buffet food often sits for hours at a lukewarm temperature, which is exactly when germs multiply. Cut fruit, salads, raita, chutneys and cream or paneer dishes left out in the open are the commonest causes of stomach upsets after a function.
try: At today's function, choose dishes served steaming hot from a heated counter, skip cut fruit and salads that have been sitting out, and drink bottled or boiled water.

title: Eat a wider variety of plant foods
body: Different plant foods feed different kinds of gut bacteria, and people who eat a wide variety of them tend to have a richer mix of healthy gut bacteria. Many of us eat the same few vegetables and one kind of dal every week.
try: Count how many different plant foods you eat this week, including dals, grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts, seeds and spices, and add one you rarely eat today, such as a millet roti or a new sabzi.

title: Hepatitis B test in every pregnancy
body: Hepatitis B can pass from a mother to her baby at birth, and most babies infected this way carry the virus for life. If the mother's test is positive, a vaccine and a protective injection given to the baby soon after birth prevent most of these infections.
try: If you or someone in your family is pregnant, check the antenatal reports for an HBsAg test, and ask the doctor for it if it has not been done.

title: Measure the oil you cook with
body: Oil has more calories than any other food: one tablespoon adds about 120 calories, and pouring straight from the bottle can add several spoons without anyone noticing. Extra oil adds to weight gain and fat in the liver, even when it is a healthy oil.
try: Add oil to today's cooking with a teaspoon instead of pouring it from the bottle, and note how many days a litre lasts in your home.

title: Some medicines can cause constipation
body: Iron and calcium tablets, some strong painkillers, antacids containing aluminium and some medicines for blood pressure, allergy or mood can slow the bowel. Many people take laxatives for years without anyone checking whether a medicine is the cause.
try: If your constipation started after a new medicine, ask your doctor whether it could be the reason. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own.

title: Warm lemon water does not melt fat
body: No drink can melt body fat. Fat is lost only when you take in fewer calories than you use, and warm water with lemon simply adds water to your day. Adding honey to it adds sugar, and lemon on an empty stomach can bring on heartburn in some people.
try: Drink it if you enjoy it, without honey, and put your effort into a daily walk and smaller portions at dinner.

title: Gur and gajak are still sugar
body: Gur, gajak, chikki and til laddoo are winter favourites, and gur is often seen as a healthy sweetener. It does have traces of minerals, but it is mostly sugar and raises blood sugar much like white sugar, which matters for diabetes and fatty liver.
try: Keep today's winter sweet to one small piece after a meal, and count gur as sugar if you are watching your weight or blood sugar.

title: Go easy on white butter this winter
body: Makki roti and sarson ka saag often come with a big lump of white butter or ghee in winter. Butter and ghee are rich in saturated fat and calories, and large helpings every day add to weight gain, fatty liver and high cholesterol.
try: Keep today's butter or ghee to one level teaspoon on your plate, and enjoy the saag for its own taste.

title: Acidity tablets work best before breakfast
body: The common acid-lowering tablets, whose names usually end in -prazole, switch off the stomach's acid pumps, which become active when food arrives. Taken 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast they work well, while taken after food or at random times they often seem to fail.
try: If you have been prescribed one, take it before breakfast with water, and ask your doctor before continuing it beyond the advised course.

title: Pale stools with dark urine need checking
body: Bile from the liver gives stool its brown colour. Stools that turn pale, grey or clay-coloured, especially with dark urine, yellow eyes or itching, can mean bile is not reaching the gut because of a liver problem or a blocked bile duct.
try: Glance at the colour of your stool and urine today. If stools stay pale for more than two or three days, or a baby passes pale stools, see a doctor without delay.

title: Make soup at home, skip the packet
body: Winter evenings call for soup, and instant packet soups are quick to make. Most are high in salt and thickened with cornflour, with very little vegetable in them. A home-made soup of tomato, lauki, palak or moong dal gives fibre and nutrients with far less salt.
try: Make a pot of vegetable or dal soup today, season it lightly, and keep the packets for emergencies.

title: Swallowed acid or cleaner: go to hospital
body: Toilet cleaners, acids and drain openers can badly burn the mouth, food pipe and stomach. Making the person vomit, or giving milk, salt water or other home remedies, can add to the damage. An early endoscopy at a hospital shows how much injury there is and guides treatment.
try: Keep every cleaner in its original labelled bottle, never in a water or cold-drink bottle, and lock it away from children. If someone swallows one, rinse the mouth with water and go to a hospital straight away.

title: Health drink powders are mostly sugar
body: Many malt and chocolate powders sold for children's growth and strength list sugar among their first ingredients. A daily glass can add several teaspoons of sugar, which builds a sweet habit and adds to weight gain and fatty liver, even in children. Plain milk with balanced meals gives most children the protein and calcium they need.
try: Read the label of the health drink at home today. If sugar is among the first three ingredients, cut the scoop down slowly and move towards plain milk.

title: Ask about the hepatitis A vaccine
body: Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water and is a common cause of jaundice in India. Young children usually recover well, but in adults and in people with existing liver disease it can be severe. A vaccine is available and gives long-lasting protection.
try: Check your child's vaccination card for hepatitis A today, and if you have a liver condition, ask your doctor whether you need the vaccine too.
